COUNTRIES.name: DR Congo
COUNTRIES.summary: Largest copper producer in Africa and roughly 70% of world cobalt. Eastern provinces contested by M23/AFC; the mining belt in Lualaba and Haut-Katanga is far from the front but exposed to export policy swings and border congestion.

Kasumbalesa border throughput and Lobito rail ramp-up
Washington and Doha peace tracks with Rwanda / M23
Manono lithium licence dispute (AVZ v. Zijin)
calendar: Lobito Atlantic Railway targets higher copper volumes; Zambia link financing

COUNTRIES.name: Zambia
COUNTRIES.summary: Second-largest African copper producer with a stated goal of 3 Mt/y by 2031. Policy has been investor-friendly since 2021; power supply and transport capacity are the binding constraints.
watch: Post-election policy continuity after the August 2026 general election (verify outcome)
Hydropower deficit at Kariba and tariff for mines
Lobito rail extension to the Copperbelt
Mopani and Konkola restart trajectories
calendar: General election held (desk to confirm result and transition)
Zambia Lobito rail link financing decisions

COUNTRIES.name: Zimbabwe
COUNTRIES.summary: Africa's largest lithium producer and the second-largest PGM producer. Government pushes in-country processing through export bans; currency and sanctions on individuals complicate payments.
watch: Lithium concentrate export ban scheduled for January 2027
ZiG currency stability and forex retention rules
Succession politics within ZANU-PF

COUNTRIES.name: South Africa
COUNTRIES.summary: Deepest mining jurisdiction on the continent and the main outlet for the Copperbelt by road. Rail and port underperformance at Transnet and US tariff exposure are the live issues; politics stable under the coalition government.
watch: Transnet rail volumes and private-operator access
US tariffs and AGOA status
Mining charter and energy policy under the GNU
calendar: Local government elections window opens (to be scheduled)
Transnet concession awards on key export lines

COUNTRIES.name: Guinea
COUNTRIES.summary: World's largest bauxite exporter and, with Simandou, a new top-tier iron ore source. Military-led government has revoked licences and reshaped the bauxite sector; civilian legitimacy contested.
watch: Simandou ramp-up and Trans-Guinean railway reliability
Further bauxite licence revocations and local refining demands
Political consolidation after the December 2025 election

COUNTRIES.name: Mali
COUNTRIES.summary: Fourth-largest African gold producer under a military government that rewrote the mining code in 2023 and took direct control of Loulo-Gounkoto in 2025. Jihadist fuel blockades reached Bamako in late 2025.
watch: Barrick settlement implementation and state share of Loulo-Gounkoto (verify current status)
JNIM pressure on fuel and road corridors to Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire
Goulamina lithium exports and state participation
calendar: Transition timeline; junta leader granted renewable five-year term in 2025

COUNTRIES.name: Ghana
COUNTRIES.summary: Africa's largest gold producer with a stable democracy. State gold-buying agency GoldBod now centralises small-scale gold purchases; crackdown on illegal mining continues.
watch: GoldBod export rules and effect on refiners
Ewoyaa lithium project permitting
Manganese (Nsuta) export policy

COUNTRIES.name: Tanzania
COUNTRIES.summary: Gateway port for the Copperbelt via Dar es Salaam and TAZARA, and a gold producer. Post-election violence in late 2025 showed political risk is higher than its reputation suggests.
watch: Dar es Salaam port throughput under DP World concession
TAZARA revamp timeline (Chinese financing)
Kabanga nickel development

COUNTRIES.name: Mozambique
COUNTRIES.summary: Beira, Maputo and Nacala corridors serve Zimbabwe, Zambia and Malawi. Post-election unrest shut the Maputo corridor repeatedly in 2024-25; insurgency persists in Cabo Delgado near Balama graphite.
watch: Cabo Delgado security and Balama operations
Beira corridor rail and port capacity
Opposition mobilisation around budget and fuel prices

COUNTRIES.name: Angola
COUNTRIES.summary: Host of the Lobito Corridor, the shortest route from the Copperbelt to the Atlantic. Fuel-subsidy protests in 2025 were deadly; the port and railway are the strategic assets to watch.
watch: Lobito Atlantic Railway volumes and Zambia extension
Fuel-price protests and urban unrest
2027 election positioning

COUNTRIES.name: Namibia
COUNTRIES.summary: Stable jurisdiction with the Walvis Bay corridor as an alternative outlet for the Copperbelt. Export ban on unprocessed lithium and other critical minerals in force since 2023.
watch: Walvis Bay corridor uptake
Critical minerals beneficiation rules

COUNTRIES.name: Gabon
COUNTRIES.summary: Second-largest manganese ore exporter. The 2023 coup leader won the 2025 election; government intends to ban manganese ore exports from 2029 to force local processing.
watch: Manganese export-ban timeline and Comilog processing investment
Transgabonais railway reliability
calendar: Planned ban on manganese ore exports

COUNTRIES.name: Burkina Faso
COUNTRIES.summary: Military government nationalising gold assets through SOPAMIB; insurgents control large parts of the territory. Part of the Alliance of Sahel States outside ECOWAS.
watch: Further nationalisations under the 2024 mining code
Security of mine sites and supply roads
Gold sales channels and refinery plans

COUNTRIES.name: Niger
COUNTRIES.summary: Nationalised the Somaïr uranium mine from Orano in 2025. Junta aligned with Mali and Burkina Faso; export routes through Benin and Nigeria politically constrained.
watch: Disposal of stranded uranium stocks
Border policy with Benin
Gold and oil revenue politics

COUNTRIES.name: Côte d'Ivoire
COUNTRIES.summary: Fast-growing gold producer and the main coastal outlet for Mali and Burkina Faso via Abidjan and San Pedro. President re-elected for a fourth term in October 2025.
watch: Northern border security with Mali and Burkina Faso
Port capacity at Abidjan and San Pedro

COUNTRIES.name: Botswana
COUNTRIES.summary: Stable democracy with a growing copper belt (Khoemacau, Motheo). Change of government in 2024 passed without disruption.
watch: Kalahari copper belt expansion
Trans-Kalahari corridor to Walvis Bay

COUNTRIES.name: Sierra Leone
COUNTRIES.summary: Iron ore (Tonkolili) and rutile exporter with contested elections and periodic licence disputes.
watch: Tonkolili export rail and port capacity
Licence stability

COUNTRIES.name: Liberia
COUNTRIES.summary: Iron ore exporter via Buchanan; third-party rail access for Guinean ore is a live policy dispute.
watch: Rail access for Guinean iron ore (HPX / Ivanhoe Atlantic)
ArcelorMittal concession terms

COUNTRIES.name: Rwanda
COUNTRIES.summary: Transit and processing hub for eastern DRC tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold. Sanctions on officials over support for M23 raise compliance risk for any cargo routed through Kigali.
watch: US and EU sanctions scope
Peace deal implementation and mineral traceability requirements

COUNTRIES.name: Uganda
COUNTRIES.summary: Gold refining and re-export hub with origin-of-gold questions; long-serving president re-elected in January 2026.
watch: Gold export traceability and refinery audits
Northern Corridor congestion

COUNTRIES.name: Senegal
COUNTRIES.summary: Dakar is Mali's main port; stable politics, strained public finances.
watch: Dakar–Bamako corridor security
Debt restructuring

COUNTRIES.name: Kenya
COUNTRIES.summary: Mombasa anchors the Northern Corridor to Uganda, Rwanda and eastern DRC. Recurrent youth-led protests since 2024.
watch: Protest cycles around budget
Northern Corridor rail and road performance

COUNTRIES.name: Cameroon
COUNTRIES.summary: Contested October 2025 election; Mbalam-Nabeba iron ore and Kribi port are the metals angle. Anglophone conflict persists.
watch: Post-election stability and succession
Mbalam rail and Kribi mineral terminal

COUNTRIES.name: Madagascar
COUNTRIES.summary: Military took power in October 2025 after youth protests. Ambatovy nickel-cobalt and graphite exports continue but policy direction is unclear.
watch: Transition roadmap and mining code review
Ambatovy ownership and financing

COUNTRIES.name: Sudan
COUNTRIES.summary: Civil war since April 2023. Gold funds both sides and leaves largely through informal channels to the Gulf. No formal corridor is reliable.
watch: Gold smuggling routes and sanctions exposure for Gulf refiners
Port Sudan control

COUNTRIES.name: Ethiopia
COUNTRIES.summary: Gold producer with regional conflicts (Amhara, Tigray tensions) and a dispute with Eritrea over sea access.
watch: Eritrea tensions
Mining licence reforms

COUNTRIES.name: Nigeria
COUNTRIES.summary: Africa's largest crude exporter by capacity and, since the Dangote refinery reached full rate in 2026, a net exporter of refined products. Pipeline sabotage and theft in the Niger Delta remain the main physical risk; emergency rule in Rivers State in 2025 showed how quickly politics reaches the pipelines.
watch: Dangote crude sourcing and product export volumes
Trans Niger and Trans Forcados pipeline security
NNPC refinery restarts and subsidy politics
2027 general election positioning

COUNTRIES.name: Libya
COUNTRIES.summary: Two rival authorities and armed groups that can close a field or a valve at will. Output swings between 1.2 million b/d and half that within weeks; 2026 brought a Sharara pipeline shutdown and force majeure at Zawiya, then valve closures at Hamada and Tahara.
watch: Sharara–Zawiya pipeline and force majeure status
Central bank and revenue disputes between Tripoli and Benghazi
Guard and militia closures at NC fields
Greenstream gas flows to Italy
calendar: Elections repeatedly postponed; no firm date

COUNTRIES.name: Algeria
COUNTRIES.summary: Europe's third-largest gas supplier through Transmed, Medgaz and the Arzew and Skikda LNG plants. Politically stable under tight state control; contract terms are set by Sonatrach and shift with Algiers' diplomatic moods.
watch: Pipeline gas volumes to Italy and Spain
Relations with Morocco and Spain affecting Medgaz
Upstream licensing round results

COUNTRIES.name: Egypt
COUNTRIES.summary: Owner of the Suez Canal and SUMED pipeline, and now a gas importer after Zohr declined. The 2025 Israel–Iran war cut Israeli gas supply and forced LNG imports through floating terminals; Suez revenue tracks Red Sea security.
watch: Suez Canal transit recovery
Israeli gas deliveries and LNG import tenders
Foreign-exchange availability for fuel imports
calendar: Zohr and West Delta decline-management milestones

COUNTRIES.name: Mauritania
COUNTRIES.summary: New LNG exporter since the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project's first cargo in 2025, and a long-standing iron ore exporter through SNIM. Stable by Sahel standards; security risk is spillover from Mali.
watch: GTA phase 2 decisions
SNIM iron ore volumes via Nouadhibou
Sahel spillover on the eastern border

COUNTRIES.name: Equatorial Guinea
COUNTRIES.summary: Declining oil producer trying to keep the Punta Europa LNG plant fed with gas from neighbouring fields. Long-serving ruler; succession and governance risk dominate.
watch: Gas supply to Punta Europa (Alen, Aseng, cross-border)
Succession politics

COUNTRIES.name: Congo-Brazzaville
COUNTRIES.summary: Oil producer with new floating LNG exports from the Marine XII block. Heavily indebted; contract and payment risk more than security.
watch: Congo LNG second phase volumes
Debt restructuring and fuel payment arrears

COUNTRIES.name: Chad
COUNTRIES.summary: Landlocked producer exporting through the Chad–Cameroon pipeline to Kribi. Nationalised ExxonMobil's former assets in 2023; Sudan's war spills over the eastern border.
watch: Pipeline tariff disputes with Cameroon
Sudan spillover and refugee flows
Arbitration over the 2023 nationalisation

COUNTRIES.name: South Sudan
COUNTRIES.summary: All crude leaves through Sudan's pipeline to Port Sudan, so Sudan's war controls South Sudan's income. Exports stopped in 2024, resumed at reduced rates in 2025, and remain hostage to the fighting.
watch: Bashayer pipeline and Port Sudan security
Peace deal implementation and elections
Arrears to Chinese and Malaysian operators

COUNTRIES.name: Morocco
COUNTRIES.summary: No domestic refining since 2015; Tangier Med is the main bunkering and transshipment hub at the Gibraltar gateway. Low political risk; relevance is logistics.
watch: Tangier Med capacity and bunker supply
Nigeria–Morocco gas pipeline progress

COUNTRIES.name: Brazil
COUNTRIES.summary: The world's second-largest iron ore exporter and a 3.5 million b/d pre-salt oil producer. Policy risk is incremental rather than abrupt: tax changes, licensing delays and tailings-dam rules. The October 2026 general election sets the tone for Petrobras pricing, the Equatorial Margin and mining royalties.
watch: Post-election direction on Petrobras fuel pricing and the Equatorial Margin (desk to confirm result)
Vale's Carajás expansion and dam-safety decommissioning schedule
US tariff regime on Brazilian goods and the exemption list
Rail and port capacity at Ponta da Madeira and Santos
calendar: General election, first round (runoff 25 October); desk to confirm outcome
Petrobras drilling results on FZA-M-59, Equatorial Margin

COUNTRIES.name: Argentina
COUNTRIES.summary: Vaca Muerta has turned Argentina into a crude exporter and, from 2027, a prospective LNG exporter; the Puna hosts the second-largest lithium pipeline in the triangle. The RIGI incentive regime (2024) anchors large projects, but currency controls, provincial politics and the 2027 presidential cycle keep regulatory risk elevated.
watch: RIGI approvals for copper (Vicuña, Los Azules) and lithium projects
Peso regime and export-duty changes
VMOS pipeline and Punta Colorada terminal timeline
Southern Energy FLNG first cargo (target 2027)

COUNTRIES.name: Chile
COUNTRIES.summary: Largest copper producer in the world and second in lithium. Institutions are strong; the live risks are permitting time, water, grade decline at Codelco and the state's role in lithium through the Codelco–SQM joint venture. The government that took office in March 2026 has promised faster permitting (verify programme).
watch: Permitting reform implementation and project timelines
Codelco output recovery after the El Teniente accident
Codelco–SQM lithium JV and new salar tenders
Water and desalination constraints in the north
calendar: Codelco structural projects: Chuquicamata underground, El Teniente new mine level

COUNTRIES.name: Peru
COUNTRIES.summary: Second-largest copper producer with a chronically unstable presidency: seven presidents since 2016. The mining belt works despite the politics, but the southern road corridor from Las Bambas is blocked several times a year and informal gold mining (REINFO) is now a security problem. The 2026 general election produced a new government in July (desk to confirm).
watch: Las Bambas corridor blockades and the REINFO formalisation deadline
New administration's mining and security posture (inaugurated 28 July 2026, verify)
Chancay port ramp-up and Cosco exclusivity
Norperuano pipeline attacks and Petroperú finances

COUNTRIES.name: Bolivia
COUNTRIES.summary: Holder of the largest lithium resource and producer of almost none of it. Twenty years of MAS rule ended in November 2025; the new government inherits a dollar shortage, fuel queues and declining gas output. Lithium contracts with Chinese and Russian partners await legislative approval.
watch: Ratification of YLB lithium contracts (CBC, Uranium One)
Fuel import financing and diesel shortages
Gas export volumes to Brazil and Argentina
Exchange-rate unification

COUNTRIES.name: Colombia
COUNTRIES.summary: Declining oil and gas producer with the region's most active insurgent threat to pipelines. The Petro government froze new exploration licences and Colombia became a gas importer; the 2026 election (31 May, runoff 21 June) decides whether that policy reverses (desk to confirm result). US relations deteriorated sharply in late 2025.
watch: New government's stance on exploration licensing (inaugurated 7 August 2026, verify)
ELN attacks on Caño Limón–Coveñas and Catatumbo security
Gas import capacity at Cartagena and Buenaventura
US sanctions exposure after the October 2025 designations

COUNTRIES.name: Venezuela
COUNTRIES.summary: Largest oil reserves in the world and output under one million b/d. The January 2026 US operation that removed Maduro left an interim administration negotiating sanctions relief licence by licence (verify current status). Every cargo depends on an OFAC authorisation, and the grid, refineries and upgraders are degraded.
watch: OFAC general licences and who may lift crude
Interim government stability and election timetable
Orinoco upgrader throughput and Jose terminal loadings
Gold exports from the Orinoco Mining Arc

COUNTRIES.name: Guyana
COUNTRIES.summary: Fastest-growing oil producer in the world: Stabroek passed 900,000 b/d in 2025 with Yellowtail and heads towards 1.3 million b/d by 2027. Politics are stable after the September 2025 election; the external risk is Venezuela's Essequibo claim.
watch: Uaru (2026) and Whiptail (2027) start-ups
ICJ ruling on the Essequibo case and Venezuelan posture
Gas-to-energy project and local content rules
Gold mining permits and Omai restart
calendar: Whiptail first oil; Stabroek towards 1.3 million b/d

COUNTRIES.name: Ecuador
COUNTRIES.summary: Oil exporter whose two trunk pipelines run through landslide country, and whose coast is now a cartel battleground. The Noboa government is pro-investment but faced a month-long national strike in 2025 over fuel subsidies. Mirador and Fruta del Norte anchor a growing mining sector.
watch: SOTE and OCP pipeline integrity and force majeure declarations
Cartel violence around Guayaquil and Esmeraldas
Mining consultation rules and Cascabel permitting
Fuel subsidy policy and protest risk

COUNTRIES.name: Panama
COUNTRIES.summary: The canal and a closed copper mine. Cobre Panamá has been shut since the Supreme Court voided its contract in November 2023; the government has allowed preservation work and is negotiating a path to reopen. Canal transits recovered from the 2023–24 drought, but water remains the constraint and the ports concession is caught between Washington and Beijing.
watch: Cobre Panamá reopening terms and First Quantum arbitration
Gatún Lake levels through the dry season (January–April)
Panama Ports / CK Hutchison concession outcome
Río Indio reservoir project
calendar: Dry season begins; draft restrictions possible if Gatún is low

COUNTRIES.name: Trinidad and Tobago
COUNTRIES.summary: The Caribbean's LNG and petrochemical hub, short of gas. Atlantic LNG runs below capacity; the Dragon cross-border field with Venezuela was blocked when OFAC revoked its licence in April 2025, and its future depends on Caracas–Washington relations.
watch: Dragon and Manakin-Cocuina cross-border gas licences
Atlantic LNG train utilisation
Deepwater exploration results (bp, Shell)
Alignment with US policy on Venezuela

COUNTRIES.name: Suriname
COUNTRIES.summary: Next Guyana, five years behind: GranMorgu (Block 58) reached FID in 2024 and targets first oil in 2028. Gold is the current export; a new government took office in July 2025 with a debt restructuring behind it.
watch: GranMorgu construction progress and local content
Staatsolie financing of its 20% stake
Gold mining regulation and Rosebel/Merian output

Southern Chad fields exporting through the Chad–Cameroon pipeline.
Offshore loading terminal at the end of the Chad–Cameroon pipeline.

Import point for East Africa's refined products; government-to-government supply deal with Gulf suppliers.
One of two remaining South African crude refineries after SAPREF's closure; restarted 2025 after a 2020 fire.

Largest port in Africa by capacity; bunker and transshipment hub at the Gibraltar gateway.
Largest copper mine in the world, roughly 1.2–1.3 Mt/y. Water comes from desalination; the main risks are labour contracts and grade.
High-grade operation near the Bolivian border; the Anglo–Teck merger (2025) brings it together with Quebrada Blanca under one owner (verify completion).

High-altitude heap leach in San Juan; glacier-law litigation history.

Extra-heavy crude requiring diluent and upgraders; output fluctuates with naphtha imports and power.
Main crude export terminal and upgrader complex; loadings track OFAC licences almost cargo by cargo.
955,000 b/d nameplate running at a small fraction after fires, outages and a lack of parts.
Largest offshore gas field in Latin America; licences for exports to Colombia and Trinidad have been floated.
Cross-border gas field meant to feed Trinidad's LNG; OFAC revoked the licence in April 2025 (status under review, verify).
Four trains restructured into a single facility in 2023; runs well below 15 Mt/y capacity for lack of gas.
Ammonia and methanol complex competing with LNG for gas.
Gas and liquids from the Amazon piped over the Andes; feeds Peru LNG and Lima.
Only LNG export plant on the Pacific coast of the Americas.
Rebuilt at great cost; Petroperú's debt crisis is the risk to its operation.
110,000 b/d, chronic outages; sits beside the SOTE export terminal at Balao.
200,000 b/d refinery; Colombia's main product exporter and gas-import point.
Mature Arauca field whose pipeline is the most-attacked piece of infrastructure in the Americas.
Largest Bolivian gas field, in decline; exports to Argentina ended in 2024.
US$10.5 billion FID in October 2024; 220,000 b/d FPSO with first oil targeted 2028.
One of two Chilean refineries; Chile imports most of its crude.
Import terminal supplying central Chile; dependence rose as Argentine pipeline gas fluctuated.
Private port handling pre-salt crude transshipment and Minas-Rio iron ore.

Bulk port for coal, chrome and ferroalloys; PGM concentrates and manganese also move here.
Dedicated iron ore terminal fed by the Sishen line.
Manganese export terminal; capacity expansions planned.
Efficient alternative to Durban for Zambian and Botswanan copper; longer road leg.
Atlantic end of the Lobito Corridor; mineral terminal operated under the Lobito Atlantic Railway concession.
Main eastern outlet for the Copperbelt by road and TAZARA; DP World concession since 2023.
Serves Zimbabwe and Zambia; rail and road corridor via Mutare.
Chrome, ferrochrome and magnetite from South Africa; closed repeatedly by unrest in 2024-25.
Deep-water port linked by rail to Malawi and Tete.
Northern Corridor gateway to Uganda, Rwanda and eastern DRC.
Bauxite export port for CBG and neighbouring mines.
New deep-water iron ore port for Simandou.
Main port for Mali and Burkina Faso traffic; gold and lithium concentrate.
Secondary Ivorian port; manganese and nickel.
Mali's traditional port; rail to Bamako largely defunct, road dominant.
Manganese terminal at the end of the Transgabonais railway.
Deep-water port; planned mineral terminal for Mbalam iron ore.
Contested during the civil war; gold leaves mainly by air and informal routes.
River port serving Kinshasa; marginal for Katanga metals.
Iron ore export port for SNIM; fishing and bunkering.
Container and product import hub; Lekki deep-sea port serves Dangote exports.
Northern entrance of the Suez Canal.
Southern entrance of the Suez Canal.
Also a bunker and offshore-support base for Orange Basin drilling.
Largest port in Latin America; containers, grains and some ore.
Vale's Carajás iron ore terminal; the largest ore port in the Americas.
Vale's southern iron ore and pellet terminal fed by the Vitória–Minas railway.
Iron ore and container port in Sepetiba Bay.
Alumina and bauxite port for Alunorte; also grains.
Main Peruvian port; concentrates from the central belt by rail.
Outlet for Las Bambas, Cerro Verde and Quellaveco concentrates.
Cosco-controlled deepwater port opened November 2024; direct services to Shanghai.
Copper cathode and concentrate port; also the outlet for Argentine and Bolivian lithium via Jama.
Concentrate and acid port north of Antofagasta.
Chile's largest container port; copper from El Teniente.
Transit port for Bolivian mineral exports under the 1904 treaty.
Crude, LPG and grain port; end of the Oldelval pipeline.
Paraná river port complex; draft limits in low-water years.
Container and product port beside the Reficar refinery; LNG import terminal.
Crude export terminal at the end of the Caño Limón and Ocensa pipelines.
Main Pacific port; security problems in the city.
Largest Venezuelan general cargo port; product imports.
Shallow river port; offshore oil is lifted directly from FPSOs.
Crude export terminal for SOTE and OCP.

Pacific entrance to the canal; container transshipment.

CORRIDORS.name: Lobito Corridor
CORRIDORS.note: Concession to Lobito Atlantic Railway (Trafigura, Mota-Engil, Vecturis) with US DFC and EU backing. Fastest route to the Atlantic for Kolwezi copper; capacity still a fraction of road volumes. Zambian spur (Chingola–Jimbe) in financing.

CORRIDORS.name: North–South Corridor
CORRIDORS.note: The workhorse route: most Copperbelt cathode and concentrate still goes by truck to Durban through Kasumbalesa, Chirundu and Beitbridge. Each border adds days; Zimbabwe fuel and currency rules add cost.

CORRIDORS.name: Dar es Salaam Corridor
CORRIDORS.note: TAZARA rail plus the Tunduma road crossing. China agreed a US$1.4bn revamp of TAZARA; until delivered, trucks dominate. Dar port under DP World since 2023 with improving dwell times.

CORRIDORS.name: Beira Corridor
CORRIDORS.note: Shortest sea access for Zimbabwe PGM and lithium concentrate; Forbes/Machipanda border and Beira draft limits constrain volumes.

CORRIDORS.name: Walvis Bay–Ndola–Lubumbashi
CORRIDORS.note: Politically the calmest route out of the Copperbelt, via Kazungula bridge and Namibia's Trans-Caprivi highway. Longer road leg, but reliable port with spare capacity.

CORRIDORS.name: Sangaredi–Kamsar bauxite rail
CORRIDORS.note: CBG's dedicated line; shared-use demands and licence revocations elsewhere in Boké are the policy risk.

CORRIDORS.name: Trans-Guinean Railway
CORRIDORS.note: New heavy-haul line and port built for Simandou; single-asset dependency makes any failure or political dispute a full-stop for exports.

CORRIDORS.name: Mali gold & lithium outlets
CORRIDORS.note: Gold leaves Mali mostly by air to Dubai; fuel, consumables and lithium concentrate move by road from Dakar and Abidjan. JNIM blockaded fuel convoys in late 2025, the clearest test of this corridor's fragility.

CORRIDORS.name: Northern Corridor
CORRIDORS.note: Carries inputs into eastern DRC and 3T and gold out through Uganda and Rwanda. Cargo touching M23-controlled areas or sanctioned intermediaries is a compliance problem.

CORRIDORS.name: Bushveld–Richards Bay rail
CORRIDORS.note: Transnet Freight Rail performance decides PGM concentrate and ferrochrome throughput; private operator access is opening slowly.

CORRIDORS.name: Transgabonais railway
CORRIDORS.note: Single line carrying nearly all of Gabon's manganese; derailments have halted exports for weeks at a time.

CORRIDORS.name: Sishen–Saldanha iron ore line
CORRIDORS.note: Heavy-haul line with chronic locomotive shortages; export volumes have run below nameplate for years.

CORRIDORS.name: Gulf to Bab el-Mandeb
CORRIDORS.note: The tanker lane carrying about a fifth of world oil and LNG. Closed from late February 2026 by the US–Israel conflict with Iran; reopened to commercial traffic in designated lanes on 17 April 2026 under a truce, with a US blockade on Iranian ports continuing. Flows slow to normalise.

CORRIDORS.name: Red Sea – Suez route
CORRIDORS.note: September 2026 Suez transits were 1,228 (second month above 100m dwt) but still 39% below pre-crisis levels; Bab el-Mandeb 47% below. Houthis attacked a containership off Yemen on 7 October 2026 and announced a blockade of Saudi Red Sea ports. Most Suez tankers carry Russian crude to India.

CORRIDORS.name: Cape of Good Hope diversion
CORRIDORS.note: The default alternative when the Red Sea is unsafe; adds roughly two weeks and raises bunker consumption. Carriers began switching back to Suez through 2026.

CORRIDORS.name: Mediterranean – Atlantic lane
CORRIDORS.note: Libyan and Algerian crude, Algerian LNG and Mediterranean products to the Atlantic; Tangier Med bunkering at the exit.

CORRIDORS.name: Gulf of Guinea export lane
CORRIDORS.note: West African crude and Dangote products to Europe, Asia and the US Gulf; piracy and kidnapping risk concentrated off the Niger Delta.

CORRIDORS.name: EACOP (East African Crude Oil Pipeline)
CORRIDORS.note: Heated 216,000 b/d line from Lake Albert to Tanga; 82% complete in April 2026 with first oil targeted for the second half of 2026. Financing and litigation pressure from campaigners continues.

CORRIDORS.name: Chad–Cameroon pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Chad's only export route; tariff disputes between N'Djamena and Yaoundé and the 2023 nationalisation of Exxon's stake are the live issues.

CORRIDORS.name: Transmed gas pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Largest Algerian gas route to Italy via Tunisia; volumes rose after Europe cut Russian supply.

CORRIDORS.name: Medgaz pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Direct Algeria–Spain line; the Maghreb–Europe line via Morocco has been shut since 2021 over the Algeria–Morocco dispute.

CORRIDORS.name: Greenstream pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Libya's gas export line to Italy; exposed to the same western-Libya instability as Zawiya.

CORRIDORS.name: SUMED pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Bypasses the Suez Canal for crude; throughput rises and falls with Red Sea security and Gulf flows.

CORRIDORS.name: Niger Delta pipelines (TNP / TFP)
CORRIDORS.note: Trans Niger and Trans Forcados lines: theft, sabotage and explosions (March 2025 TNP blast) regularly halt Bonny Light and Forcados exports.

CORRIDORS.name: Greater Nile pipeline (South Sudan–Port Sudan)
CORRIDORS.note: South Sudan's only outlet runs through Sudan's civil war; a 2024 rupture halted exports for months and flows have been partial since.

CORRIDORS.name: Niger–Benin pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Niger's only crude export route, opened 2024. Benin blocked loadings during the 2024 border dispute and attacks on the line have interrupted flows since.

CORRIDORS.name: Kenya Pipeline (Mombasa–Nairobi–Eldoret)
CORRIDORS.note: Carries imported refined products inland for Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and eastern DRC; capacity constraints push volumes onto trucks.

CORRIDORS.name: Sharara–Zawiya crude line
CORRIDORS.note: Libya's most-interrupted pipeline: shut by blockades repeatedly and again on 14 August 2026, cutting national output by about a fifth and triggering force majeure at Zawiya.

CORRIDORS.name: Panama Canal
CORRIDORS.note: About 5% of world seaborne trade. The 2023–24 drought cut daily transits from 36 to 24 and imposed draft limits; levels recovered in 2024–25. LNG and LPG carriers from the US Gulf to Asia are the most price-sensitive users.

CORRIDORS.name: Strait of Magellan / Cape Horn
CORRIDORS.note: Route for vessels too large for the canal and for Vaca Muerta crude heading to the Pacific; pilotage compulsory, winter weather closes windows.

CORRIDORS.name: Southern mining corridor (Las Bambas road)
CORRIDORS.note: Unpaved stretches through Chumbivilcas and Espinar communities who block the road over dust, compensation and land; MMG has lost months of shipments in bad years. Informal miners joined the blockades in 2025.

CORRIDORS.name: Lithium triangle roads (Paso de Jama)
CORRIDORS.note: Carbonate from Jujuy and Catamarca crosses the Andes at 4,200 m to Chilean ports; snow closures and customs at Jama add days.

CORRIDORS.name: Carajás railway (EFC)
CORRIDORS.note: Vale's heavy-haul line moving about 180 Mt/y; occasional blockades by communities and the MST, and a court-ordered stoppage in 2024 over indigenous consultation.

CORRIDORS.name: Vitória–Minas railway
CORRIDORS.note: Vale's southern system; concession renewed to 2057 with investment obligations.

CORRIDORS.name: Minas-Rio slurry pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Longest iron ore slurry pipeline in the world; pipeline leaks in 2018 shut the operation for most of a year.

CORRIDORS.name: Oleoducto Norperuano
CORRIDORS.note: Petroperú's 1970s line across the Amazon and Andes; dozens of spills, many from deliberate cuts by communities seeking compensation. Volumes are small but politically loud.

CORRIDORS.name: Caño Limón–Coveñas pipeline
CORRIDORS.note: Bombed more than 1,000 times by the ELN since the 1980s; the Catatumbo offensive of January 2025 brought renewed attacks and a state of emergency.

CORRIDORS.name: SOTE and OCP pipelines
CORRIDORS.note: Both trunk lines cross the Coca river gorge, where regressive erosion since 2020 has repeatedly broken them. The March 2025 rupture spilled into the Esmeraldas river and forced a force majeure on exports.

CORRIDORS.name: Oldelval and VMOS (Vaca Muerta export system)
CORRIDORS.note: Oldelval's Duplicar expansion lifted capacity in 2025; the VMOS line to a new deepwater terminal at Punta Colorada (Río Negro) is due in 2027 and would allow VLCC loadings.

CORRIDORS.name: Bolivia–Brazil gas pipeline (GASBOL)
CORRIDORS.note: Bolivian volumes have fallen with field decline; Argentina has begun sending Vaca Muerta gas to Brazil through Bolivia in reverse flow.

CORRIDORS.name: Orinoco Belt to Jose
CORRIDORS.note: Diluted crude moves by pipeline to the Jose upgraders and loading berths; throughput depends on naphtha imports, power and OFAC licences.

CORRIDORS.name: Brazil–Asia ore lane (via Cape)
CORRIDORS.note: Valemax and Capesize vessels carry about 300 Mt/y of Brazilian ore to China round the Cape; freight is the swing cost against Australian ore.

CORRIDORS.name: Trans-Pacific concentrate lane
CORRIDORS.note: Most Chilean and Peruvian concentrate goes to Chinese smelters; Chancay's direct Shanghai service cut transit to 23 days.

CORRIDORS.name: Caribbean crude lane
CORRIDORS.note: Venezuelan cargoes to the US run under OFAC licences; the shadow fleet heads east. US naval activity in the southern Caribbean from late 2025 added interdiction risk for unlicensed liftings.

CHOKES: Busiest mineral border in Africa; truck queues of several days are routine when DRC export paperwork or Zambian systems stall.
Upgraded one-stop post, still the slowest leg on the North–South Corridor at peak.
One-stop border on the Zambezi; delays tied to Zimbabwean fuel levies and system outages.
Gateway to Dar es Salaam; congestion when TAZARA is down.
Modern bridge opened 2021; low-friction route to Walvis Bay.
Beira corridor crossing; narrow road and periodic closures.
Closed repeatedly by Mozambican unrest in late 2024; chrome and magnetite exports rerouted.
Under M23 control since January 2025; any cargo is a sanctions and traceability risk.
Rail border on the Lobito Corridor; customs harmonisation still maturing.
Main fuel and goods entry for Mali; convoys targeted by JNIM in 2025.
Closed from late February 2026 by the Iran conflict; reopened 17 April in designated lanes under a truce. About a fifth of world oil and LNG passes here.
Houthi attacks since 2023; September 2026 transits still 47% below pre-crisis. Containership fired on 7 October 2026.
Transits recovering (1,228 in September 2026) but 39% below pre-crisis; revenue critical to Egypt.
Low-risk gateway; Tangier Med bunkering on the southern shore.
Diversion route; weather and bunker availability at Cape Town and Durban are the practical constraints.
Lane for Mozambique LNG and Beira/Nacala cargoes; piracy low, cyclone season risk.
Kidnap-for-ransom hotspot; incidents fell after 2021 but armed guards and routing still cost money.
Transits recovered from the 2023–24 drought; Gatún Lake level is the variable to watch every dry season.
Pilotage compulsory; winter weather closes windows for a day or two at a time.
Lithium and Bolivian cargo crossing at 4,200 m; snow closures in winter.
Main Andean crossing; closed dozens of days a year by snow, with truck queues on both sides.
Bolivian cargo to Peruvian ports; protests close it for weeks in bad years.
Bolivian mineral exports to Arica; customs and truckers' strikes.
Reopened to trade in 2022; ELN and Venezuelan colectivo activity, and political closures at short notice.
Route for Caribbean crude to the US Gulf; Haitian instability raises small-vessel risk only.
Narrow channel between Trinidad and the Orinoco delta; Venezuelan naval presence and smuggling.
Paraná – Río de la Plata channel
Dredged river channel; low water in drought years limits drafts for grain and crude exports from Rosario.

ZONES.name: Eastern DRC (Kivus, Ituri)
ZONES.note: M23/AFC control of Goma and Bukavu; ADF and militia activity north.

ZONES.name: Central Sahel
ZONES.note: JNIM and ISSP insurgency across Mali, Burkina Faso and western Niger; fuel blockades and convoy attacks.

ZONES.name: Cabo Delgado
ZONES.note: Islamist insurgency near graphite and LNG projects.

ZONES.name: Sudan war
ZONES.note: SAF–RSF civil war; gold economy informalised.

ZONES.name: Anglophone Cameroon
ZONES.note: Separatist conflict in North-West and South-West regions.

ZONES.name: Red Sea and Gulf of Aden
ZONES.note: Houthi anti-shipping campaign; attacks resumed in 2026 after a pause.

ZONES.name: Gulf / Hormuz
ZONES.note: Iran conflict zone; mines and restricted lanes after the 2026 closure.

ZONES.name: Niger Delta
ZONES.note: Pipeline sabotage, theft and militancy; emergency rule in Rivers State 2025.

ZONES.name: Libya (rival authorities)
ZONES.note: Tripoli and Benghazi governments; armed groups can close fields and terminals.

ZONES.name: Catatumbo and Arauca
ZONES.note: ELN and FARC dissident offensive since January 2025; pipeline attacks and displacement on the Venezuelan border.

ZONES.name: Venezuela transition
ZONES.note: Interim administration after the January 2026 US operation; armed colectivos, degraded grid, sanctions enforcement.

ZONES.name: Southern Peru mining corridor
ZONES.note: Community blockades and informal-miner protests from Apurímac to Puno.

ZONES.name: Ecuador coastal cartel zone
ZONES.note: Guayaquil and Esmeraldas port cities under cartel violence; state of exception renewed repeatedly.

ZONES.name: Essequibo dispute
ZONES.note: Venezuelan claim to two-thirds of Guyana; ICJ case pending, military posturing on the border.

ZONES.name: Madre de Dios illegal gold
ZONES.note: Informal gold mining, mercury pollution and organised crime along the Interoceanic highway.

EVENTS: US replaces Zimbabwe sanctions programme with targeted designations
OFAC lifted the country-wide programme and designated President Mnangagwa and associates under Global Magnitsky. Compliance screening of state-linked counterparties remains necessary.
Burkina Faso takes Boungou and Wahgnion gold mines into state company SOPAMIB
Formal nationalisation of two producing mines under the 2024 mining code, with limited compensation. Template for Sahel resource nationalism.
Kariba drought cuts Zambian hydropower; mines import power and run diesel
Power rationing raised copper unit costs through the 2024-25 dry season and delayed expansions.
Resolute Mining CEO detained in Bamako
Released after Resolute agreed a US$160m settlement with the government; signalled that executives are leverage in code renegotiations.
Post-election protests close Ressano Garcia border repeatedly
Opposition protests blocked the N4 corridor and Maputo port access through January 2025; South African chrome, ferrochrome and magnetite rerouted to Richards Bay.
Ganfeng-operated mine began production; road export via Côte d'Ivoire.
Barrick suspends Loulo-Gounkoto after Mali seizes gold stock
About three tonnes of gold removed from site by authorities; operations halted pending resolution of the dispute over the 2023 code.
M23/AFC captures Goma; Bukavu falls in February
Rwandan-backed rebels took the two largest cities in the Kivus. Northern Corridor cargo into eastern DRC and 3T exports now pass through rebel-taxed territory.
US sanctions Rwandan minister Kabarebe and M23 spokesman
Treasury designations for support to M23 and illicit mineral trade; EU followed with its own listings. Due-diligence burden rises on Kigali-routed cargo.
DRC suspends all cobalt exports for four months
ARECOMS halted cobalt hydroxide exports to lift prices after a 2024 collapse. Stocks built at mines and at Durban and Dar es Salaam.
Oligui Nguema elected president of Gabon
Coup leader of 2023 won the election with about 90% of the vote; policy continuity on manganese beneficiation expected.
Seismic activity halts Kakula underground mine
Ivanhoe suspended underground operations at Kakula and cut 2025 guidance; partial restart over following months.
Zimbabwe sets lithium concentrate export ban from January 2027
Government confirmed a deadline for in-country processing; Chinese operators accelerate sulphate plant construction.
Mali court places Loulo-Gounkoto under provisional state administration
Court-appointed administrator took control with authority to restart operations and sell gold.
Orano's majority stake expropriated; stockpiled yellowcake stranded by closed Benin border. Arbitration initiated.
DRC extends cobalt export suspension by three months
Extension to late September 2025; traders report hydroxide stocks of several months of demand.
DRC and Rwanda sign US-brokered peace agreement in Washington
Agreement paired with a prospective US–DRC minerals partnership; implementation and M23 withdrawal unresolved.
Taxi strike over diesel subsidy cuts turned into days of unrest with more than 20 deaths; Lobito port operations unaffected but political risk repriced.
US imposes 30% tariff on South African goods; AGOA lapses in September
Metals largely exempt or treated separately, but the broader trade relationship and investment sentiment weakened.
Guinea withdraws GAC bauxite mining licence
Government revoked Emirates Global Aluminium's licence citing unmet refinery commitments, after cancelling dozens of smaller permits earlier in the year.
JNIM blockades fuel deliveries to Bamako
Insurgents attacked fuel convoys from Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire; weeks of shortages, school closures and mine supply constraints.
Guinea approves new constitution by referendum
Cleared the path for the junta leader to stand in the December election.
Cameroon election: Biya declared winner, opposition protests
Contested result and deadly protests; succession uncertainty for a 92-year-old president.
Military takes power in Madagascar after youth protests
President left the country; an army officer assumed the presidency. Mining policy under review.
DRC replaces cobalt ban with export quotas
Annual cap of about 96,600 t for 2026 and 2027, allocated by producer; ARECOMS controls allocation and can revise.
Ouattara re-elected for a fourth term
Low-turnout election with main rivals excluded; continuity for port and mining policy.
Tanzania election violence and internet shutdown
Protests after a one-sided election; Dar es Salaam port and road freight disrupted for several days.
Simandou loads first iron ore shipment
First export from Morebaya port via the Trans-Guinean railway; ramp-up to 120 Mt/y planned over several years.
Barrick and Mali reach settlement on Loulo-Gounkoto (reported)
Reported agreement including a payment by Barrick and return of the complex to company control. Desk flags: verify terms and operating status.
Transition formally ends with the junta leader as elected president; investor terms on bauxite and iron ore now set by his administration.
Museveni re-elected in Uganda amid opposition crackdown
Continuity for the Northern Corridor and gold refining sector; protests contained.
Multi-day truck queues at Kasumbalesa as copper exports hit record
Border systems and quota paperwork slowed clearance; queues of 20–30 km reported on the Zambian side.
Transnet reports modest rail recovery; Durban dwell times still above target
Volumes improved from the 2023 low but remain well below the 2017 peak; private operator slots awarded on selected lines.
Lobito Atlantic Railway reports rising copper volumes
Operator cites more frequent trains from Kolwezi and new rolling stock; still a small share of DRC exports.
Strait of Hormuz closure sends bunker fuel to ~US$1,000/t
Middle East conflict closed the strait; marine fuel prices more than doubled and Africa–Asia freight rates spiked. Singapore traders reported absorbing costs on pre-signed contracts.
Radiant World iron ore trader in distress; lenders withdraw
Singapore-based trader laid off staff amid a police inquiry; court later removed the founder's control. Counterparty risk case for African ore offtakes.
Withdrawal took effect in January 2024 after quota disputes; frees Angola to pursue output growth from new blocks.
Congo LNG ships first cargo from Tango FLNG
Eni's fast-track floating plant began exports; a second, larger unit followed in 2025.
Benin blocks Niger crude loadings at Sèmè amid border dispute
Cotonou halted exports through the new Niger–Benin pipeline during the post-coup standoff; loadings resumed later in 2024 but remain hostage to politics.
Woodside's FPSO delivered the country's first oil; output ramped to about 100,000 b/d.
Eastern Libyan government orders oil fields shut over central bank dispute
Output fell by more than half for weeks until a deal on the central bank governorship; template for how Libyan politics reaches exports.
South Sudan exports resume via Port Sudan at reduced rates
Repairs to the war-damaged pipeline allowed partial resumption after the 2024 shutdown; flows remain exposed to Sudan's fighting.
Trans Niger Pipeline explosion; emergency rule declared in Rivers State
A blast on the TNP halted Bonny Light flows and the federal government suspended the state government the next day; security of delta pipelines repriced.
Greater Tortue Ahmeyim exports first LNG cargo
bp and Kosmos' floating project made Mauritania and Senegal LNG exporters.
Tripoli clashes; NOC warns of force majeure
Fighting between armed groups in the capital raised the risk to western terminals and the Greenstream line.
Israel–Iran war halts Israeli gas to Egypt; LNG imports surge
Egypt leased additional floating import terminals and tendered for dozens of cargoes as Leviathan and Karish shut in temporarily.
US$35bn Leviathan gas supply deal with Egypt signed
Largest export contract in Israel's history, tying Egypt's power supply to the Israeli pipeline link.
All onshore and offshore activities resumed after the 2021 force majeure; 4,000 workers mobilised and first LNG targeted for 2029.
US–Israel conflict with Iran effectively closes the Strait of Hormuz
War from 28 February 2026 stopped most commercial transits of the lane carrying a fifth of world oil and LNG; prices spiked and Africa–Asia freight repriced.
Uganda and Tanzania target first crude exports from Tanga in the second half of 2026; farmers' lawsuit filed in London the next day.
Iran reopens Hormuz to commercial traffic in designated lanes under truce
Transit limited to lanes Iran deems safe; US blockade of Iranian ports maintained pending a deal. Shipowners cautious over possible mines.
Dangote refinery sustains 700,000 b/d in performance tests
Above nameplate; Nigeria now supplies most of its own fuel and exports products, reshaping Atlantic product flows.
Houthi threat to Saudi-bound shipping; five tankers turn back in the Red Sea
Renewed threats after a lull; owners resumed Cape diversions for Saudi-linked cargoes.
Sharara–Zawiya pipeline shut; force majeure on Zawiya loadings
Libyan output fell from about 700,000 to 560,000 b/d; responsibility for the stoppage unclear; a 600,000-barrel Sharara loading was cancelled.
Guards close valve, halting Hamada, Tahara and NC5
NOC called the closure illegal and warned of force majeure if repeated; motives undisclosed.
Suez transits reach 1,228 in September, still 39% below pre-crisis
Second consecutive month above 100m dwt; containers returning from the Cape; bulk carriers reversed on Black Sea security.
Containership fired upon off Yemen; Houthis announce blockade of Saudi Red Sea ports
Attack coincided with fighting around Mocha and strikes on Aden; not claimed. Insurers re-rated the southern Red Sea.
Panama's Supreme Court voids the Cobre Panamá contract; mine shut

The ruling ended operations at a mine producing about 1.5% of world copper after weeks of national protest. First Quantum began arbitration; the government later approved a preservation plan while negotiating terms for any restart.
Panama Canal cuts daily transits to 24 as drought drains Gatún Lake
Restrictions that began in 2023 reached their tightest point in January 2024, pushing LNG and LPG carriers to the Cape and Suez. Transits normalised later in 2024 as rains returned.
Argentina enacts the RIGI large-investment incentive regime
Thirty-year tax and foreign-exchange stability for projects above US$200 million; the basis for Vaca Muerta export infrastructure and the next generation of copper and lithium mines.
US$10.5 billion final investment decision for a 220,000 b/d FPSO; first oil targeted 2028.
Chancay port inaugurated with Xi Jinping present
Cosco's deepwater port north of Lima opened direct services to Shanghai, cutting transit to about 23 days and giving Peru and northern Chile a new outlet for concentrates.
Bolivia signs lithium extraction contracts with Uranium One and CBC
Direct-lithium-extraction deals with Russian and Chinese partners for Uyuni, each needing congressional approval that stalled through 2025.
ELN offensive in Catatumbo displaces tens of thousands; state of emergency
Fighting with FARC dissidents spread along the Venezuelan border; pipeline attacks and road closures followed, and the government suspended peace talks with the ELN.
The wind-down removed the main licensed outlet for Venezuelan crude to the US Gulf; a restricted licence was reissued in July 2025 allowing operations without cash payments to the government.
SOTE pipeline rupture spills crude into the Esmeraldas river
A landslide broke the trunk line; Petroecuador declared force majeure on exports and the city of Esmeraldas lost its water supply for days.
OFAC revokes the Dragon gas field licence
The cross-border field with Venezuela was Trinidad's main hope for new LNG feed gas; revocation left Atlantic LNG short and tied the project to US–Venezuela politics.
Southern Energy consortium commits to Argentina's first floating LNG export unit
Pan American Energy, YPF, Pampa, Harbour and Golar chartered the Hilli Episeyo for 20 years off Río Negro, targeting first exports in 2027 (date of decision: verify).
Codelco–SQM lithium joint venture takes effect
The state took majority control of the Atacama contract through 2060 after regulatory clearances in Chile and China (completion date: verify).
Informal miners block the Las Bambas corridor for weeks over REINFO
Miners demanding an extension of the formalisation registry blocked the southern corridor; MMG warned of shipment delays and declared it could not meet contracts on time.
United States imposes a 50% tariff on most Brazilian goods
The order, framed around the prosecution of former president Bolsonaro, exempted a list of products including energy and some raw materials; Brazilian exporters diverted to Asia.
Rock collapse at El Teniente kills six; sections of the mine suspended
A seismic event in the Andesita sector; the regulator halted parts of the mine and Codelco's 2025 guidance fell. Partial resumption followed under conditions.
The fourth FPSO took Guyana past 900,000 b/d; Uaru and Whiptail follow in 2026–27.
Continuity for the oil regime and the Exxon consortium; the opposition fragmented.
Anglo American and Teck agree an all-share merger
The combination puts Collahuasi and Quebrada Blanca under one owner with plans to share infrastructure; approvals pending into 2026 (verify completion).
Congress removes President Boluarte; José Jerí sworn in
The seventh presidency since 2016. A state of emergency in Lima followed; the April 2026 election went ahead on schedule.
Ibama licenses Petrobras to drill the Equatorial Margin
After five years of refusals, the environmental agency approved exploration well FZA-M-59 off Amapá, the test of whether Guyana's play extends into Brazil.

The new government took office on 8 November 2025 facing fuel queues and a dollar shortage; it promised to unblock lithium contracts and court investment.
Month-long national strike over the diesel subsidy ends
CONAIE's protests closed roads in the highlands and Amazon from 22 September; Petroecuador reported lost output and the government held the subsidy cut.
OFAC designates President Petro and family members
The designation followed US decertification of Colombia's drug effort; banks tightened screening of state-linked counterparties, though Ecopetrol itself was not listed.
Milei's party wins the midterm elections
A stronger legislative position for the reform programme and the RIGI regime; the peso regime remained the open question for investors.
José Antonio Kast wins Chile's presidential runoff
Mandate for faster permitting and a harder line on security; took office in March 2026 (verify programme details).

The most consequential political event for Venezuelan oil since 2019. Sanctions relief followed licence by licence rather than wholesale; PDVSA's physical constraints did not change overnight (desk flags all details for verification).

New general licences widened who may lift and pay for Venezuelan crude; US Gulf refiners resumed cargoes while Asian buyers waited for clarity (verify scope and dates).

A fragmented first round; the new president took office on 28 July 2026. Desk to confirm the outcome and the new administration's mining posture.

FORECASTS.q: DRC cobalt export quota regime still in force on 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES if ARECOMS quotas (or a successor volume cap) remain legally in force on the date.
FORECASTS.why: The regime is working for Kinshasa: prices recovered and the state gained allocation power. Lifting it would need a price collapse or a deal with China. Risk is quota revision rather than removal.

FORECASTS.q: Lobito Corridor moves more than 500 kt of copper and cobalt in calendar 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on operator or DRC customs data showing combined Cu + Co volumes above 500,000 t for 2027.
FORECASTS.why: Volumes are rising but rolling stock, Dilolo customs and mine-side loading remain bottlenecks. Most cargo still trucks to Durban and Dar.

FORECASTS.q: Zimbabwe enforces the lithium concentrate export ban by 31 March 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES if concentrate exports are prohibited in practice (no general exemptions) by the date; a blanket delay resolves NO.
FORECASTS.why: Government has held the line publicly and Chinese operators are building sulphate plants, but a weak lithium price makes a phased delay plausible.

FORECASTS.q: Loulo-Gounkoto operates without a new state-ordered stoppage through 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves NO if Malian authorities suspend operations, seize output or reinstate administration for more than 14 days.
FORECASTS.why: A settlement was reported in late 2025, but the junta has shown it will reopen terms when revenue needs rise. Status should be verified before use.

FORECASTS.q: Guinea revokes at least one more bauxite mining licence held by a foreign operator by 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on an official revocation of a producing or advanced bauxite licence.
FORECASTS.why: Refinery commitments remain unmet across the sector and the new administration has used revocation as leverage repeatedly.

FORECASTS.q: M23/AFC withdraws from Goma by 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES if Congolese state authority is restored in Goma under the Washington or Doha framework.
FORECASTS.why: Agreements exist on paper; neither side has moved on the ground. Withdrawal would require a security guarantee Kinshasa cannot yet provide.

FORECASTS.q: Burkina Faso nationalises an additional foreign-owned gold mine by 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on transfer of majority control of a producing mine to SOPAMIB or another state entity.
FORECASTS.why: The state is cash-constrained and the 2024 code enables it, but it also needs operators who can run the remaining mines.

FORECASTS.q: Kasumbalesa truck queues exceed five days in any month of H1 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on credible reporting (industry body, major operator or press) of average clearance times above five days in any calendar month.
FORECASTS.why: Record copper volumes meet unchanged border capacity. Lobito and Dar relief is real but gradual.

FORECASTS.q: South Africa's Transnet rail volumes exceed 170 Mt in FY2026/27
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on Transnet's reported annual freight rail tonnage.
FORECASTS.why: Recovery from the 2023 trough is slow; locomotive availability and cable theft persist. Private slots help at the margin.

FORECASTS.q: Angola's 2027 election passes without protests that close Lobito port for more than 48 hours
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves NO if the port or railway terminal is shut by unrest for over two consecutive days in the election period.
FORECASTS.why: 2025 fuel protests were serious but concentrated in Luanda; Lobito's political economy depends on the corridor staying open.

FORECASTS.q: EACOP loads its first export cargo at Tanga by 31 March 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on an official or press-confirmed first crude lifting from Tanga.
FORECASTS.why: 82% complete in April 2026 with first oil targeted for late 2026; commissioning of a heated line and the Tilenga ramp-up usually slip a quarter or two.

FORECASTS.q: Strait of Hormuz suffers another closure of seven or more days before 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES if commercial tanker transits stop or fall below 20% of normal for seven consecutive days.
FORECASTS.why: The April 2026 reopening holds but the underlying deal is unfinished and the US blockade continues; a breakdown is plausible but both sides have strong reasons to keep the lane open.

FORECASTS.q: Suez Canal monthly transits exceed 1,500 in any month of H1 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on Suez Canal Authority or Lloyd's List data showing more than 1,500 transits in a calendar month.
FORECASTS.why: September 2026 was 1,228 and 39% below pre-crisis; recovery is real but Houthi threats returned in July and October 2026.

FORECASTS.q: Libya declares force majeure at a major field or terminal again before 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on an NOC force majeure declaration covering any field or terminal above 100,000 b/d.
FORECASTS.why: Two separate shutdowns in August and September 2026 and no resolution of the political split; the base rate is several per year.

FORECASTS.q: Mozambique LNG reports no new force majeure or security suspension through 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves NO on any announced suspension of site activities of 14 days or more.
FORECASTS.why: Restart in January 2026 followed security assurances; Cabo Delgado violence persists at lower levels and the site is heavily guarded.

FORECASTS.q: Niger–Benin pipeline exports flow without a stoppage longer than 30 days in H1 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves NO on any reported interruption of loadings at Sèmè exceeding 30 consecutive days.
FORECASTS.why: Benin–Niger relations remain poor and the line has been attacked; CNPC has strong incentives to keep cargoes moving.

FORECASTS.q: Dangote refinery exports average more than 150,000 b/d of refined products in Q1 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on Kpler/Vortexa or NNPC data showing average product exports above 150,000 b/d for the quarter.
FORECASTS.why: 700,000 b/d tests in mid-2026 and domestic demand of roughly 450,000 b/d leave room for large exports, but crude sourcing and maintenance cycles are unproven.

FORECASTS.q: Cobre Panamá resumes commercial copper production by 31 December 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on First Quantum reporting concentrate shipments from the mine under a new agreement with the government.
FORECASTS.why: Both sides want the revenue, but the 2023 ruling, a new contract needing legislative approval and the arbitration make a two-year timeline tight.

FORECASTS.q: The Las Bambas corridor is blocked for 14 or more consecutive days before 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on MMG or Peruvian government confirmation of a continuous road blockade of 14+ days affecting concentrate transport.
FORECASTS.why: Blockades of this length happened in most recent years; the REINFO dispute and a new government's early months are classic triggers.

FORECASTS.q: Venezuelan crude exports to the United States exceed 300,000 b/d in any month of H1 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on EIA or Kpler data showing US imports of Venezuelan crude above 300,000 b/d for any calendar month.
FORECASTS.why: Licences have widened since early 2026 and Gulf refiners want the heavy barrels, but upgrader throughput and politics in Caracas are unreliable (desk to update as the picture clarifies).

FORECASTS.q: Panama Canal keeps average daily transits at 34 or more through the 2027 dry season (to 30 April 2027)
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves NO if the Canal Authority announces transit caps below 34 per day or draft limits below 44 ft for 14+ days.
FORECASTS.why: Gatún Lake levels recovered in 2024–25 and the authority now manages water more conservatively; a strong El Niño would be the risk.

FORECASTS.q: Argentina loads its first LNG export cargo by 31 December 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on a confirmed LNG cargo loaded from an Argentine FLNG unit.
FORECASTS.why: The Hilli Episeyo charter and pipeline works are on a 2027 schedule; floating units slip less than onshore plants, but Argentine permitting and gas supply contracts could add a quarter or two.

FORECASTS.q: Bolivia's legislature ratifies at least one YLB lithium extraction contract by 30 June 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on legislative approval of the CBC, Uranium One or any successor DLE contract.
FORECASTS.why: The new government wants investment, but the contracts were negotiated by its predecessor and Potosí civic groups oppose them.

FORECASTS.q: Petrobras announces a commercial discovery on the Equatorial Margin by 31 December 2027
FORECASTS.crit: Resolves YES on a Petrobras declaration of commerciality or a discovery notice describing hydrocarbons in commercial quantities from FZA-M-59 or an adjacent well.
FORECASTS.why: The geology is promising by analogy with Guyana, but one well rarely proves a play and drilling only began in late 2025.

BRIEFINGS.title: Baseline brief: where African metals risk stands
BRIEFINGS.lede: Issue 00 sets the desk's starting view across the five flows this platform tracks. Later issues report changes against this baseline.
sections: Copperbelt exports

The DR Congo–Zambia copper belt is producing at record rates and the roads out have not grown with it. Kasumbalesa clears tens of thousands of trucks a month and backs up whenever Congolese export paperwork changes. The Lobito railway is the structural fix, but it is still a small share of volume; Dar es Salaam and Walvis Bay absorb the rest of the overflow. The cobalt quota regime introduced in October 2025 is now the single largest policy variable for anyone holding hydroxide: allocations are political, and revisions can arrive with days of notice.
Sahel gold

Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have moved from renegotiation to direct control. The Loulo-Gounkoto episode showed a government willing to seize bullion and detain executives to force terms; Burkina Faso's SOPAMIB and Niger's Somaïr nationalisation are the same logic. The operational risk is now as serious as the legal one: the 2025 fuel blockade of Bamako demonstrated that JNIM can choke the road corridors from Dakar and Abidjan, and every mine in the region runs on trucked diesel.
Guinea

Simandou has begun shipping and the bauxite sector has been reshaped by licence revocations. The new civilian-labelled administration is the same leadership that revoked GAC's licence, so expect continued use of permits as leverage for local refining. Single-asset dependency on the Trans-Guinean railway is the physical risk.
Southern Africa processing

Zimbabwe's lithium concentrate ban (January 2027) and Gabon's planned manganese ore ban (2029) share a theme with Namibia's existing rules: governments want processing on-shore and are prepared to lose export volume to get it. South Africa's constraint is different: it is physical, in Transnet's rail and ports, and it ripples north because Durban is the default outlet for the Copperbelt.
Eastern DRC and compliance

M23 holds Goma and Bukavu and taxes the coltan trade; the Washington agreement has not changed that on the ground. Cargo through Rwanda and Uganda now carries a sanctions and traceability burden that did not exist two years ago. For a trader, the exposure is documentary as much as physical.
What we are watching to year-end

Cobalt quota allocations for 2027; the aftermath of Zambia's August election; whether Mali's settlement with Barrick holds; freight costs if the Hormuz disruption persists into the northern winter; and any Transnet concession awards. Our open forecast calls on each are on the Forecasts tab.

BRIEFINGS.title: Energy baseline: Africa, the Mediterranean and the lanes between
BRIEFINGS.lede: The energy desk's starting view across the flows this engine tracks: Gulf and Red Sea sea lanes, North African gas and crude, the Gulf of Guinea, and East Africa's new export projects.
sections: Sea lanes

2026 rewrote the risk map. The Iran conflict closed Hormuz from late February and reopened it in designated lanes from 17 April under a truce that is still unfinished. The Red Sea recovered through the summer, then Houthi threats returned in July and an attack off Yemen in October. Suez transits in September were the best since the crisis began and still 39% below normal. For a trader the practical result is two freight regimes, Suez and Cape, that can swap within a week.
Libya

The country produces 1.2 million b/d when nobody closes a valve, and in 2026 somebody did twice: the Sharara–Zawiya line on 14 August (force majeure at Zawiya, output down a fifth) and the Hamada–Tahara valve on 15 September. Eastern terminals kept loading. Our standing forecast is that another force majeure is more likely than not within six months.
Nigeria

Dangote changes the Atlantic. At 650,000–700,000 b/d the refinery makes Nigeria a net product exporter and cuts European gasoline exports to West Africa. The delta remains the physical risk: the Trans Niger explosion and Rivers State emergency rule in 2025 showed how fast politics and pipelines connect.
North African gas

Algeria is Europe's reliable southern supplier through Transmed and Medgaz; Libya's Greenstream is the fragile one. Egypt has flipped from exporter to importer as Zohr declines, and the 2025 Israel–Iran war showed how dependent Cairo is on the Israeli link and on spot LNG.
East Africa

EACOP was 82% built in April 2026 with first oil targeted for late 2026; Mozambique LNG restarted in January after five years, with first cargo in 2029; GTA made Mauritania and Senegal LNG exporters in 2025. These are the new flows, and each depends on a single pipeline or plant.
What we are watching

Hormuz truce negotiations and the US blockade; Red Sea insurance and routing after the October attack; Libya's Sharara line; EACOP commissioning; and whether Mozambique LNG's security holds. Open calls on each are on the Forecasts tab.

BRIEFINGS.title: South America baseline: copper, lithium, iron ore and the new Atlantic oil
BRIEFINGS.lede: The desk's starting view on the region's flows: Andean copper and lithium to Asia, Brazilian ore round the Cape, Vaca Muerta and the Guyana–Suriname basin, and the Caribbean lanes that sanctions reshaped.
sections: Copper

Chile and Peru supply about 40% of world mine output and the risks are physical and local rather than national: a collapsed sector at El Teniente, a blocked road out of Las Bambas, a permit that takes six years. Panama's closed mine is the one true policy shock in the region and its restart is a political negotiation. The Anglo–Teck merger consolidates the north Chilean district; Vicuña in Argentina is the next large project if RIGI holds.
Lithium

The triangle has three jurisdictions and three models: Chile's state-partnered contracts, Argentina's provincial concessions under RIGI, and Bolivia's state monopoly that still produces almost nothing. Prices are low, so the risk is to project timelines rather than to existing cargo. Watch Bolivia's legislature and any Chilean move to tender new salars.
Iron ore

Vale moves about 300 Mt/y to China round the Cape; it is the most reliable large flow in this engine, with court-ordered rail stoppages and dam decommissioning as the known interruptions. The US tariff on Brazil mattered more politically than for ore, which flows east.
Oil

Guyana is the growth story, at over 900,000 b/d and rising, with Suriname five years behind. Brazil's pre-salt is the volume, and the Equatorial Margin well is the option. Argentina's shale crude exports are growing with Oldelval and will step up when VMOS opens in 2027. Venezuela is the wildcard: after the January 2026 operation, every cargo depends on a licence and the physical system is degraded; treat all Venezuelan data as provisional.
Lanes

The Panama Canal is a water story: 2023–24 showed what a drought does to LNG and LPG routing. The Caribbean crude lane now carries interdiction risk for unlicensed liftings. The Magellan route matters for Vaca Muerta crude to the Pacific and for ships too large for the canal.
What we are watching

Peru's and Colombia's new governments and Brazil's post-election cabinet; the Las Bambas road; Cobre Panamá talks; OFAC's Venezuela licences; Gatún Lake levels from January; and Argentina's first LNG cargo. Open calls are on the Forecasts tab.

DEMAND.name: United States
DEMAND.links: Imports heavy crude from Canada, Mexico and (under licence) Venezuela; Gulf refiners are the natural home for Orinoco barrels. Small residual demand for Nigerian light sweet. Largest product exporter to Latin America and West Africa, now displaced in Nigeria by Dangote.

DEMAND.name: China
DEMAND.links: The buyer that sets African and Brazilian crude prices: largest customer for Angola, Congo, Gabon and South Sudan, and for Brazilian pre-salt. Demand flattened in 2024 as EVs and LNG trucks cut gasoline and diesel; petrochemical feedstock still grows. Also the destination for most Chilean and Peruvian copper concentrate.

DEMAND.name: India
DEMAND.links: Fastest-growing large consumer. Reliance and Nayara took Russian barrels; Nigerian and Angolan light sweet remain regular, and Guyanese crude has entered the slate. Indian refiners are the swing buyer for West African cargoes when China steps back.

DEMAND.name: Saudi Arabia
DEMAND.links: Exporter, but a large consumer through power burn and refining. Yanbu and the East-West pipeline are the bypass when Hormuz closes, as in spring 2026.

DEMAND.name: Russia
DEMAND.links: Sanctioned exporter competing with West African and Latin American grades for Indian and Chinese refiners; the shadow fleet it created now also serves Venezuela and Iran.

DEMAND.name: Japan
DEMAND.links: Structural decline. Almost entirely Gulf crude, so Hormuz is the exposure; LNG from Mozambique and Nigeria matters more than crude from Africa.

DEMAND.name: South Korea
DEMAND.links: Gulf-dependent refiner with growing African and US light grades for petrochemicals; buyer of Mozambique and Nigerian LNG and Chilean copper.

DEMAND.name: Brazil
DEMAND.links: Net crude exporter, net product importer. Pre-salt output rises faster than domestic refining, so exports to China grow; diesel imports come from the US Gulf and, increasingly, Russia.

DEMAND.name: Canada
DEMAND.links: Heavy crude exporter to the US; the Trans Mountain expansion (2024) opened Pacific exports to Asia that compete with Latin American heavy grades.

DEMAND.name: Germany
DEMAND.links: Declining demand. Replaced Russian pipeline crude with Norwegian, US, Kazakh and West African grades; Libyan and Nigerian cargoes land at Wilhelmshaven and Rotterdam.

DEMAND.name: Iran
DEMAND.links: Exports under sanctions almost entirely to China via the shadow fleet; the 2026 conflict and US blockade cut both exports and domestic supply.

DEMAND.name: Mexico
DEMAND.links: Exports Maya heavy crude and imports most of its gasoline and diesel from the US; Pemex's Dos Bocas refinery is slowly changing that.

DEMAND.name: Indonesia
DEMAND.links: Growing importer of crude and products; Pertamina buys Nigerian, Angolan and Saudi crude and Singapore products.

DEMAND.name: Singapore
DEMAND.links: Consumption is mostly refinery throughput and bunkering: the largest bunker port in the world and the pricing hub for Asian products, including those moving to East Africa.

DEMAND.name: France
DEMAND.links: Historically the largest European buyer of West and North African crude; TotalEnergies' African upstream (Nigeria, Angola, Uganda, Mozambique) links its refineries to this engine's assets.

DEMAND.name: Spain
DEMAND.links: Major buyer of Nigerian, Libyan and Algerian crude and Algerian gas via Medgaz; Repsol is active in Venezuela under licence.

DEMAND.name: United Kingdom
DEMAND.links: North Sea decline raises import needs; Nigerian and Algerian grades suit UK refineries. London remains the insurance and legal centre for the shipping these flows depend on.

DEMAND.name: Thailand
DEMAND.links: Gulf-dependent importer with occasional West African cargoes; PTT trades African crude.

DEMAND.name: Italy
DEMAND.links: Largest buyer of Libyan crude and Algerian and Libyan pipeline gas (Transmed, Greenstream); Eni operates across Libya, Algeria, Egypt, Congo, Mozambique and Côte d'Ivoire.

DEMAND.name: Turkey
DEMAND.links: Growing importer buying Russian, Iraqi and Libyan crude; STAR refinery and Tüpraş take West African grades opportunistically.

DEMAND.name: United Arab Emirates
DEMAND.links: Exporter with the Fujairah bypass pipeline outside Hormuz; Fujairah is the bunkering and storage hub for the Gulf lane and a trading base for African products.

DEMAND.name: Australia
DEMAND.links: Imports most refined products from Singapore and Korea; competes with Brazil and Guinea as an iron ore and bauxite supplier to China.

DEMAND.name: Iraq
DEMAND.links: Second OPEC exporter; Basra loadings are wholly Hormuz-dependent, which is why the 2026 closure shifted Chinese buying towards Africa and Brazil.

DEMAND.name: Taiwan
DEMAND.links: Gulf and US crude; CPC and Formosa buy occasional West African cargoes and are large Mozambique LNG off-takers.

DEMAND.name: Malaysia
DEMAND.links: Exporter of light sweet crude that competes with Nigerian grades; Pengerang refinery imports Gulf and African crude.

DEMAND.name: Netherlands
DEMAND.links: Rotterdam is the European pricing and storage hub; Nigerian, Angolan and Libyan crude land here and products leave for West Africa.

DEMAND.name: Egypt
DEMAND.links: Inside the engine as an energy jurisdiction: Suez Canal and SUMED owner, now a gas importer, with fuel imports exposed to foreign-exchange shortages.

DEMAND.name: Poland
DEMAND.links: Replaced Russian crude with Saudi, Norwegian and West African grades through Gdańsk; Orlen is an active buyer of Nigerian cargoes.

DEMAND.name: Argentina
DEMAND.links: Became a net crude exporter in 2024 on Vaca Muerta; diesel imports persist in the harvest season. In this engine as a lithium, copper and energy jurisdiction.

DEMAND.name: Vietnam
DEMAND.links: Fast-growing importer; Nghi Son refinery runs Kuwaiti crude, Binh Son buys Azeri and West African grades.
